trackTitle: Git & GitHub: From Absolute Beginner to Ultra Expert (Master Edition)
description: A comprehensive, enterprise-grade Git and GitHub mastery roadmap from absolute beginner to ultra expert level, designed for classroom learners, engineering students, and professional software engineers. Covers version control foundations, three-tree architecture, atomic commits, branch lifecycles, fast-forward vs 3-way merges, interactive rebase, cherry-pick, stash & worktree, reflog disaster recovery, submodules & subtrees, Git internals (DAG, objects, blobs, trees, commit packfiles), GitHub Actions CI/CD automation pipelines, branch protection & security scanning, monorepos, and technical interview viva prep.

segments.title: Segment 1 – Git Foundations & Local Repository Architecture (Beginner)
segments.summary: Master what Git is, distributed version control concepts, local repository initialization, the three-tree architecture (Working Tree, Staging Index, HEAD), atomic commits, history inspection, and safe undo strategies.

modules.title: Introduction to Version Control & Git Architecture
modules.summary: Understand the history and motivation for version control, centralized (SVN/CVS) vs distributed (Git/Mercurial) architectures, Linus Torvalds' design principles, cross-platform installation, and configuring global/local developer environments.
topics: What is Version Control and why software projects fail without it
Evolution of VCS: Local VCS -> Centralized VCS (SVN, CVS, Perforce) -> Distributed VCS (Git, Mercurial)
Centralized vs Distributed VCS: Single point of failure, offline working capability, and branching performance
Origins of Git: How Linus Torvalds built Git in 2005 for the Linux kernel development
Core Design Principles of Git: Speed, simple design, non-linear development support, full distribution, and data integrity
Installing Git on Windows (Git for Windows / Git Bash), macOS (Homebrew / Xcode CLI), and Linux (apt / dnf / pacman)
Configuring Git Identity: git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email
Configuring Essential Preferences: core.editor, init.defaultBranch (main vs master), and color.ui
Handling Line Endings Across Operating Systems: core.autocrlf (true on Windows, input on macOS/Linux)
Configuration Scope Hierarchy: System (--system) vs Global (--global) vs Local (--local) vs Worktree (--worktree)
Inspecting Active Configuration: git config --list --show-origin
Anatomy of the .git Directory: Overview of HEAD, objects, refs, config, hooks, and index
Classroom Dialogue: Sukanta Sir and Barrackpore students on why Git is essential for every developer
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Complete environment setup, verification, and default editor configuration
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 001_001
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between centralized and distributed version control systems
Install and configure Git globally and locally on any operating system
Understand the configuration hierarchy and diagnose configuration conflicts
Recognize the internal structure and role of the .git directory
miniProjects: Personal Developer Git Environment Setup & Verification Script
useCases: Standardizing developer environments across engineering teams
Setting up clean development machines for modern software development
commonMistakes: Using different emails across commits, causing unmatched GitHub contribution graphs
Mismatched core.autocrlf settings leading to phantom line-ending diffs across Windows and Linux teams
Editing the .git folder manually without understanding its internal invariants
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 1: Getting Started
Official Git Documentation: git-config(1)
teachingTips: Show students the hidden .git directory immediately after git init to demystify Git from day one.
Demonstrate how git config --list --show-origin pinpoints exactly which config file is overriding a setting.
preReading: Basic understanding of terminal commands (cd, ls, pwd, mkdir)

modules.title: The Three-Tree Architecture & Core Workflow
modules.summary: Master Git's famous Three-Tree Architecture (Working Directory, Staging Index, Repository/HEAD), the lifecycle of tracked/untracked files, staging techniques, crafting atomic commits with Conventional Commits, and ignoring files via .gitignore.
topics: Git's Three-Tree Architecture: Working Directory -> Staging Area (Index) -> Repository (HEAD Commit)
The Lifecycle of File Status: Untracked, Unmodified, Modified, and Staged
Creating a Local Repository: git init vs Cloning an Existing Repository (git clone)
Inspecting Working Tree Status: git status and short status format (git status -s)
Staging Changes: git add <file>, git add . vs git add -A (understanding deletions vs new files)
Interactive Staging: Staging partial file chunks using git add -p (patch mode)
Creating Commits: git commit -m vs opening full editor for descriptive multi-line commit messages
The Philosophy of Atomic Commits: One logical change per commit for bisectability and clean code reviews
Conventional Commits Specification: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, chore, build, ci
Inspecting Unstaged vs Staged Changes: git diff (working tree vs index) and git diff --staged (index vs HEAD)
Ignoring Files with .gitignore: Syntax rules, wildcards (*, ?), directory indicators (/), negation (!), and comments
Common .gitignore Templates: Node.js (node_modules), Python (__pycache__, .venv), Java (.class), and IDE files (.vscode, .idea)
Repository-Specific Local Exclusions: The .git/info/exclude file and Global gitignore (~/.gitignore_global)
Classroom Walkthrough: Sachin, Mahima, and Susmita building an Invoice Management project with atomic commits
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Initializing a project, configuring .gitignore, staging chunks with patch mode, and writing conventional commits
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 001_002
learningOutcomes: Differentiate clearly between the Working Tree, Staging Area (Index), and Repository HEAD
Stage exact changes using both full-file and interactive patch-level staging
Write clean, atomic commit messages following the industry Conventional Commits standard
Construct robust .gitignore rules to prevent accidental credential and build artifact leakage
miniProjects: Multi-File Staging & Atomic Commit Pipeline for an E-Commerce Cart Module
useCases: Structuring clean developer commits before submitting code reviews
Shielding repositories from build artifacts, secrets, and environment binaries
commonMistakes: Committing node_modules or .env files due to missing or delayed .gitignore creation
Writing vague commit messages like 'fixed stuff', 'update', or 'wip' instead of Conventional Commits
Using git add . blindly without reviewing git status or git diff first
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 2: Git Basics - Recording Changes to the Repository
Conventional Commits 1.0.0 Specification (conventionalcommits.org)
teachingTips: Teach students git add -p early so they learn to separate unrelated bug fixes from feature code into separate commits.
Show the visual diagram of the Three Trees to make the role of the Index crystal clear.

modules.title: Viewing Commit History & Inspecting Changes
modules.summary: Master repository history exploration using git log formatting, filtering by author/date/message, inspecting commit details with git show, comparing arbitrary revisions with git diff, tracking file evolution, line-by-line attribution with git blame, and string searching with the pickaxe operator.
topics: Deep Dive into git log: Default output, commit SHA-1 hashes, author vs committer metadata, and timestamps
Formatting Log Output: git log --oneline, --decorate, and graphical branching view with git log --graph --all
Custom Log Formatting with Pretty Print: git log --pretty=format:'%h %ad | %s%d [%an]' --date=short
Limiting and Filtering History: Limiting by count (-n), date ranges (--since, --until), and author (--author)
Filtering History by Commit Message: Searching messages with git log --grep
Path-Specific History: Tracking commits affecting specific files or folders (git log -- <path>)
Viewing Detailed Changes in Log: git log -p (inline diffs) and git log --stat (file modification statistics)
Inspecting Specific Commits with git show: Viewing commit metadata, parents, and patch diff for any commit hash
Comparing Revisions with git diff: Comparing Working Tree to HEAD, Index to HEAD, and arbitrary commits (git diff commitA commitB)
Line-by-Line Code Forensics with git blame: Identifying author, commit hash, and timestamp for every line in a file
Advanced git blame Filtering: Ignoring whitespace changes (-w) and restricting line ranges (-L start,end)
The Pickaxe Operator: Searching history for commits that added or removed specific code strings with git log -S 'search_string'
Tracking Renamed and Moved Files: git log --follow <file> across historical refactorings
Classroom Case Study: Debangshu and Swadeep diagnosing an unexpected production price discount calculation bug using git blame and git log -S
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Reconstructing a repository timeline, extracting author statistics, and finding deleted functions with pickaxe
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 001_003
learningOutcomes: Customize and filter git log output to quickly locate relevant commits in large codebases
Inspect full commit details and file diff statistics using git show and git diff
Perform code forensics and author attribution using git blame with whitespace filtering
Track deleted, added, or renamed functions across the entire repository lifetime using pickaxe and --follow
miniProjects: Repository History Forensics & Audit Report for a Multi-Developer Project
useCases: Auditing security vulnerabilities and identifying when a bug was introduced
Preparing release changelogs by filtering commits between milestone tags
commonMistakes: Failing to use --follow when running git log on a file that was previously renamed or moved
Using git blame without -w and getting distracted by mass-formatting changes instead of actual logic changes
Scrolling endlessly through raw git log instead of using filtering flags like --grep or -S
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 2: Viewing the Commit History
Official Git Documentation: git-log(1), git-blame(1)
teachingTips: Teach students to create a git lg alias early on: git config --global alias.lg 'log --graph --oneline --decorate --all'.
Demonstrate the power of git log -S to find when a variable was deleted from anywhere in the codebase.

modules.title: Undoing Changes, Reset, Restore & Clean
modules.summary: Master safe undo mechanisms in Git without panic: discarding working tree changes with git restore, unstaging indexed files, amending the latest commit with git commit --amend, understanding git reset modes (soft, mixed, hard), reverting shared history with git revert, and safely purging untracked files with git clean.
topics: The Decision Matrix for Undoing Changes in Git: What stage are your changes in? (Working Tree, Staging, Local Commit, Pushed Commit)
Discarding Unstaged Changes: Modern git restore <file> vs legacy git checkout -- <file>
Unstaging Staged Changes: Modern git restore --staged <file> vs legacy git reset HEAD <file>
Amending the Most Recent Commit: git commit --amend for updating messages or adding forgotten staged files
Understanding Commit Rewriting Risks: Why amending pushed commits causes diverged remote history
Demystifying git reset: How reset moves the HEAD pointer and adjusts Index and Working Tree
The Three Modes of git reset: --soft (moves HEAD only), --mixed (moves HEAD and updates Index - default), and --hard (moves HEAD, updates Index, and overwrites Working Tree)
The Golden Safety Rule of git reset --hard: Understanding what is permanently unrecoverable vs what is in Git's object store
Safe Undo for Public/Shared Branches: git revert <commit> to create a new inverse snapshot without rewriting history
Reverting Reverts and Handling Merge Commit Reverts: Overview of git revert -m 1 <merge_commit>
Cleaning Untracked Files and Directories: git clean with dry-run (-n), force (-f), recursive directory (-d), and ignored file (-x) options
Interactive Cleaning: Running git clean -i for safe step-by-step interactive pruning
Classroom Troubleshooting: Sukanta Sir guiding Abhronila and Tuhina through restoring accidentally modified database migration scripts
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Practicing git restore, commit --amend, soft/mixed/hard resets, and safe git revert
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 001_004
learningOutcomes: Choose the exact correct undo command based on the file state in the Three-Tree Architecture
Unstage files and discard working tree edits cleanly using modern git restore commands
Differentiate between git reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard with complete confidence
Safely undo commits on shared branches using non-destructive git revert
miniProjects: Accidental Deletion & Staged Error Recovery Drill Simulation
useCases: Undoing mistaken commits locally before pushing to upstream production
Reverting flawed production releases cleanly without rewriting branch histories
commonMistakes: Running git reset --hard when having uncommitted, unstaged work, resulting in unrecoverable local file loss
Using git reset on a public shared branch instead of git revert, breaking collaborator repositories
Running git clean -fd without checking git clean -nd dry-run first, deleting new un-staged source files
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 2: Undoing Things
Official Git Documentation: git-restore(1), git-reset(1), git-revert(1)
teachingTips: Always enforce the rule: 'Run git status before and after every reset or restore operation.'
Emphasize that git revert is safe for team branches, while git reset is meant for private local branches.
preReading: Module 001_002 Staging Index and HEAD concept

segments.title: Segment 2 – Branching, Merging, Rebasing & Conflict Resolution (Intermediate)
segments.summary: Master Git's lightweight branch pointer mechanics, fast-forward vs 3-way recursive merges, merge base computation, conflict detection and manual/visual resolution, linear history crafting with interactive rebase, autosquash, git stash, and multi-folder parallel workflows with git worktree.

modules.title: Branching Fundamentals & Pointer Mechanics
modules.summary: Understand what a Git branch really is (a lightweight 41-byte movable pointer to a commit object), the role of HEAD as a symbolic reference, creating and switching branches with git switch, diagnosing and fixing detached HEAD states, branch renaming/deletion, and comparing branches.
topics: What is a Branch in Git? Demystifying branches as lightweight 41-byte text pointers containing SHA-1 commit hashes
How Git Branching Differs from Other VCS: Instant zero-cost branching vs copying entire directories
The Role of HEAD: Understanding HEAD as a symbolic reference pointing to the current branch ref (.git/HEAD)
Creating Branches: git branch <branch-name> and inspecting branch pointers (.git/refs/heads/)
Switching Branches: Modern git switch <branch> vs legacy git checkout <branch>
Creating and Switching in One Step: git switch -c <branch> and git checkout -b <branch>
Listing and Inspecting Branches: git branch, git branch -v (with last commit), and git branch -vv (with upstream tracking)
Renaming Branches: git branch -m <old_name> <new_name> and renaming current branch with git branch -M <new_name>
Deleting Branches: Safe deletion with git branch -d (checks merge status) vs force deletion with git branch -D
The Detached HEAD State: What causes it (checking out a commit SHA, tag, or remote branch directly)
Navigating and Experimenting in Detached HEAD: Why commits made in detached HEAD are at risk of garbage collection
Recovering from Detached HEAD: Saving experimental commits by creating a new branch (git switch -c new_feature_branch)
Comparing Branches: git diff branchA..branchB (two-dot) vs git diff branchA...branchB (three-dot diff from merge base)
Classroom Experiment: Sachin and Mahima inspecting .git/refs/heads/ in the terminal to observe pointer movement after commits
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Creating feature branches, exploring detached HEAD, creating rescue branches, and branch cleanup
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 002_001
learningOutcomes: Explain how Git branch pointers and the HEAD reference work at the filesystem level
Create, switch, rename, and delete branches using modern git switch and git branch commands
Diagnose, experiment safely within, and recover from a Detached HEAD state
Compare differences between two branches using double-dot and triple-dot diff notation
miniProjects: Multi-Feature Branching & Pointer Lifecycle Simulation
useCases: Isolating experimental features safely without affecting stable main branch code
Managing hotfix and feature lifecycles in agile sprint development
commonMistakes: Making commits in a detached HEAD state and switching away without creating a branch, losing direct references
Attempting to delete the currently active branch with git branch -d instead of switching to another branch first
Assuming git branch copies files on disk rather than creating an instant pointer
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 3: Git Branching - Branches in a Nutshell
Official Git Documentation: git-branch(1), git-switch(1)
teachingTips: Show the contents of .git/HEAD and .git/refs/heads/main using cat or type in the terminal so students see that a branch is literally just a text file with a 40-character commit hash.
Draw the DAG on the whiteboard to visualize how HEAD moves forward with each commit.

modules.title: Merging Strategies & Resolving Merge Conflicts
modules.summary: Master Git merge mechanics: Fast-Forward merges, 3-way recursive (ORT) merges, finding the common ancestor (merge base), disabling fast-forward with --no-ff, conflict anatomy and markers, manual and visual merge tools, aborting broken merges, and squash merging feature branches.
topics: The Concept of Merging: Integrating divergent histories into a unified line of development
Fast-Forward (FF) Merges: When does Git fast-forward? (Moving the target pointer forward without creating a merge commit)
Three-Way (3-Way) Merges: Finding the Common Ancestor (Merge Base via git merge-base branchA branchB)
The Merge Commit: Understanding why a merge commit has two (or more) parent commits
Preserving Branch Topologies: Using git merge --no-ff to enforce explicit merge commits for feature tracking
What Causes Merge Conflicts? Concurrent modifications to the same lines in the same file across divergent branches
Anatomy of Conflict Markers: <<<<<<< HEAD (Current Change), ======= (Separator), and >>>>>>> feature (Incoming Change)
Step-by-Step Conflict Resolution Workflow: Identifying conflicting files via git status, reviewing diffs, editing markers, staging, and completing the merge
Using Graphical and Visual Merge Tools: Configuring git mergetool (VS Code 3-way merge editor, Meld, KDiff3)
Aborting a Merge Safely: Canceling an in-progress merge with git merge --abort to return to a clean working state
Squash Merging: Consolidating an entire feature branch's commits into a single commit using git merge --squash
Merge Strategies & Algorithms: Recursive strategy vs Modern ORT (Ostensibly Recursive's Twin) strategy in Git 2.33+
Classroom Drama: Sachin and Susmita editing the same AuthController.js file simultaneously, triggering and resolving complex merge conflicts
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Simulating divergent branches, triggering 3-way merge conflicts, visual resolution in VS Code, and verifying merge base commits
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 002_002
learningOutcomes: Distinguish between Fast-Forward merges and Three-Way recursive/ORT merge commits
Calculate the merge base common ancestor commit between two branches
Read and resolve multi-file merge conflict markers accurately without losing critical code
Utilize git merge --abort and git merge --squash for advanced branch management
miniProjects: Multi-Developer Merge Conflict Simulation & Resolution Sandbox
useCases: Integrating feature branches into main release branches safely
Resolving conflicting team pull requests during sprint integrations
commonMistakes: Accidentally leaving conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) inside code files and committing them
Panicking during a merge conflict and manually deleting files instead of running git merge --abort
Assuming fast-forward merges always happen even when divergent commits exist on both branches
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 3: Basic Branching and Merging
Official Git Documentation: git-merge(1), git-mergetool(1)
teachingTips: Have students deliberately create a merge conflict on day 1 of branching so fear of merge conflicts is eliminated forever.
Demonstrate VS Code's 'Accept Current', 'Accept Incoming', and 'Accept Both' buttons side-by-side with raw CLI conflict markers.

modules.title: Git Rebase, History Linearization & Interactive Rebase
modules.summary: Master Git Rebase mechanics: rewinding and replaying commits to maintain a clean linear history, Rebase vs Merge philosophical comparison, the Golden Rule of Rebasing, handling conflicts during rebase, interactive rebase (pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, exec), and automated fixup with autosquash.
topics: What is Git Rebase? Replaying a sequence of commits on top of a new base tip
Rebase vs Merge Philosophical Comparison: Historical Truth (Preserving merge knots) vs Clean Linear Storytelling
Step-by-Step Standard Rebase Workflow: git switch feature && git rebase main
How Rebase Works Under the Hood: Finding merge base, saving patch deltas to temporary files, fast-forwarding target branch, and reapplying commits one by one
THE GOLDEN RULE OF REBASING: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a public/shared repository branch!
Handling Conflicts During Rebase: Resolving conflicts, staging resolved files, and continuing with git rebase --continue (No git commit!)
Rebase Control Commands: git rebase --skip (discarding redundant commit) and git rebase --abort (safe bailout)
Interactive Rebase Mastery: git rebase -i HEAD~N and git rebase -i <base_commit>

Interactive Rebase Command Directives: pick (use commit), reword (edit message), edit (pause to amend files), squash (meld into previous), fixup (meld and discard message), drop (delete commit), and exec (run shell command on each step)
Reordering Commits and Splitting a Large Commit into Atomic Commits during Interactive Rebase
Squashing Work-in-Progress (WIP) and Bugfix Commits before Submitting a Pull Request
Automating Fixups with Autosquash: git commit --fixup <commit_hash> and git rebase -i --autosquash main
Classroom Deep-Dive: Sukanta Sir demonstrating how to transform a messy 12-commit feature branch into 2 pristine, review-ready conventional commits
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Linearizing a divergent feature branch, performing interactive rebase, squashing WIP commits, and testing with exec
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 002_003
learningOutcomes: Explain the technical difference between merging and rebasing on the Git commit DAG
Apply the Golden Rule of Rebasing to avoid breaking team member repositories
Perform advanced interactive rebasing (squash, fixup, reword, drop, split) with complete confidence
Utilize --fixup and --autosquash for rapid, automated commit consolidation in CI/CD workflows
miniProjects: Messy Pull Request History Cleanup & Linearization Challenge
useCases: Cleaning up private feature branches before code review submission
Keeping feature branches up-to-date with main without generating unsightly merge bubbles
commonMistakes: Rebasing a shared main branch that other engineers have already pulled, causing duplicate commit graphs
Running git commit during a rebase conflict instead of staging and running git rebase --continue
Accidentally deleting lines in the interactive rebase TODO file, which causes Git to drop those commits
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 3: Rebasing
Official Git Documentation: git-rebase(1)
teachingTips: Emphasize that during git rebase, HEAD is in a detached state for each replayed commit.
Teach students to create a backup branch (git branch backup-before-rebase) before doing their first interactive rebase.

modules.title: Git Stash & Multi-Tasking with Git Worktree
modules.summary: Master temporary context switching with git stash (saving, listing, inspecting, applying, popping, stashing untracked files, creating branches from stashes) and parallel multi-branch development in separate directories without switching branches using git worktree.
topics: The Developer Context Switching Problem: Urgent production bug arrives while in the middle of uncommitted feature work
Temporarily Shelving Changes with git stash: Default behavior (stashes staged and unstaged tracked modifications)
Naming and Labeling Stashes: git stash push -m 'WIP: Refactoring Stripe Payment Gateway'
Stashing Untracked and Ignored Files: git stash -u (--include-untracked) and git stash -a (--all)
Inspecting the Stash Stack: git stash list and inspecting patch diffs with git stash show -p stash@{0}
Restoring Stashed Work: git stash apply (preserves stash in stack) vs git stash pop (restores and removes from stack)
Restoring Staged State: Using git stash apply --index to preserve both Index and Working Tree separation
Creating a Branch Directly from a Stash: git stash branch <new_branch_name> stash@{0}
Cleaning Up Stashes: Dropping specific stashes (git stash drop stash@{N}) and clearing the entire stack (git stash clear)
Introduction to Git Worktree: The modern solution to working on multiple branches simultaneously in separate folders
Why Worktrees Beat Stashing and Switching: No need to rebuild node_modules, recompile C binaries, or wait for IDE indexers
Creating New Worktrees: git worktree add ../hotfix-branch-dir hotfix/critical-auth-patch
Managing Active Worktrees: git worktree list, removing completed worktrees with git worktree remove, and running git worktree prune
Classroom Scenario: Swadeep and Tuhina handling an urgent client bug on production while running a long React build in their main worktree
Hands-on Terminal Lab: Managing a multi-level stash stack, rescuing stash conflicts, and setting up linked Git worktrees
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 002_004
learningOutcomes: Shelve and restore uncommitted feature changes cleanly using git stash with descriptive messages
Manage the stash stack (list, inspect, apply, pop, drop, clear) without losing experimental work
Create new Git branches directly from stored stashes to resolve complex merge conflicts
Spin up, manage, and prune linked Git worktrees for parallel branch development without context switching overhead
miniProjects: Production Hotfix Interruption Simulation with Git Worktree & Stash
useCases: Switching branches quickly to review a colleague's PR without committing half-finished code
Running long automated tests or dev servers on one branch while developing on another via git worktree
commonMistakes: Forgetting to stash untracked files with -u, causing newly created files to leak into the switched branch
Accumulating dozens of unnamed stashes over months and forgetting what changes they contain
Attempting to check out the same branch in two different worktrees simultaneously (blocked by Git for safety)
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 7: Git Tools - Stashing and Cleaning
Official Git Documentation: git-stash(1), git-worktree(1)
teachingTips: Show students git worktree as a modern alternative to stashing when dealing with heavy dependencies like node_modules.
Always teach students to provide descriptive stash messages with git stash push -m.

segments.title: Segment 3 – Remote Collaboration, GitHub & Repository Governance (Intermediate to Advanced)
segments.summary: Master remote repository mechanics, network protocols (SSH vs HTTPS), remote tracking branches, upstream syncing, GitHub/GitLab collaborative workflows, Pull Requests, code reviews, branching models (Gitflow, Trunk-Based), semantic versioning, branch protection rulesets, and secret leakage prevention.

modules.title: Remote Repositories, Remotes & Network Protocols
modules.summary: Understand remote repositories, the origin convention, remote management commands, network protocols (HTTPS with Personal Access Tokens vs SSH key pairs with ssh-agent), remote tracking branches (origin/main), fetch vs pull vs pull --rebase, pushing with upstream tracking, and pruning deleted remote branches.
topics: What is a Remote Repository? Understanding origin as a default remote alias pointing to a central server
Remote Management Commands: git remote add, git remote -v, git remote rename, and git remote remove
Inspecting Remote Details: git remote show origin (tracking branches, push/pull URLs, stale branches)
Network Protocols in Git: Local file://, SSH (git@github.com:...), HTTPS (https://github.com/...), and Git protocol (git://)
HTTPS Authentication in Modern Git: GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PAT), Git Credential Manager (GCM), and token scopes
SSH Authentication Deep-Dive: Generating SSH key pairs (ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'email@domain.com'), starting ssh-agent, and adding keys
Adding Public Keys to GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket and Verifying Connection (ssh -T git@github.com)
Remote Tracking Branches: Understanding origin/main as local read-only bookmarks of remote state (.git/refs/remotes/origin/)
The Critical Distinction: git fetch (downloads objects & updates remote refs) vs git pull (fetch + merge)
Pulling with Rebase: git pull --rebase to prevent useless local merge commits during team updates
Configuring Global Pull Rebase: git config --global pull.rebase true
Pushing Branches with Upstream Tracking: git push -u origin <branch_name> (--set-upstream)
Deleting Remote Branches: git push origin --delete <branch_name> vs deleting local branch

topics: Collaboration Models: Shared Centralized Repository Model (Direct push with branch permissions) vs Fork & Pull Request Model (Open source standard)

Anatomy of a Professional Pull Request (PR): Clear title, context description, screenshots/recordings, test plan, and related issue links

modules.title: Branching Models: Gitflow, Trunk-Based, GitHub Flow & Releases
modules.summary: Master industry-standard branching strategies: Gitflow (main, develop, feature, release, hotfix), GitHub Flow (continuous deployment), Trunk-Based Development (TBD with feature flags), Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0), annotated vs lightweight tags, and publishing automated GitHub Releases with changelogs.
topics: Why Branching Strategies Matter: Avoiding merge hell, release delays, and uncoordinated deployments in large teams
Comparative Breakdown of Industry Branching Models: Gitflow vs GitHub Flow vs Trunk-Based Development vs GitLab Flow
The Gitflow Workflow: Main (production), Develop (integration), Feature branches (feature/*), Release branches (release/*), and Hotfix branches (hotfix/*)
Gitflow Step-by-Step Lifecycle: Creating a release candidate, freezing features, applying release bugfixes, merging back to both main and develop
When to Use Gitflow: Scheduled enterprise release cycles, mobile apps, and multi-version supported software
GitHub Flow: Lightweight continuous deployment workflow: 1) Branch from main, 2) Add commits, 3) Open PR, 4) Discuss & Review, 5) Deploy & Verify, 6) Merge to main
Trunk-Based Development (TBD): Short-lived branches (< 1 day), frequent small merges to trunk/main, paired with CI and Feature Flags (Feature Toggles)

Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (Breaking changes, Backwards-compatible features, Bug fixes)

Pushing and Deleting Tags: git push origin v1.0.0, pushing all tags with git push origin --tags, and deleting with git push origin --delete <tag_name>

topics: Enterprise Repository Governance: Why open write access to main is an operational risk in production systems
GitHub Branch Protection Rules: Preventing direct pushes, enforcing pull requests before merging, and requiring linear history
Configuring Required Approvals and Dismissing Stale Approvals on New Pushes
Code Ownership with CODEOWNERS: Creating .github/CODEOWNERS to automatically assign specialized team reviews for security/database folders
Enforcing Required Status Checks: Blocking merges until automated CI tests and security linters pass successfully

modules.title: Git Cherry-Pick, Patches & Selective Integration
modules.summary: Master selective commit extraction with git cherry-pick: applying single commits, ranges of commits, cherry-picking without committing (--no-commit), resolving cherry-pick conflicts, generating email-ready patch files with git format-patch, applying patches with git apply and git am, and backporting critical bugfixes across release branches.
topics: What is Git Cherry-Pick? Applying the changes introduced by one or more existing commits onto the current HEAD
Cherry-Picking a Single Commit: git cherry-pick <commit_hash> and inspecting the newly generated commit SHA
Cherry-Picking a Range of Commits: git cherry-pick commitA..commitB (exclusive A) vs commitA^..commitB (inclusive A)
Cherry-Picking Without Committing: git cherry-pick -n (--no-commit) to stage changes for inspection and modification
Handling Conflicts During Cherry-Pick: Resolving conflict markers, staging files, and running git cherry-pick --continue or --abort
Recording Original Commits: Using git cherry-pick -x to append '(cherry picked from commit ...)' to the commit message
Real-World Use Cases for Cherry-Pick: Backporting urgent bugfixes from main to older maintenance branches (e.g., v1.2-support)
Risks and Anti-Patterns of Overusing Cherry-Pick: Duplicate commits, divergent histories, and merge conflict complications later

Generating Patch Files: git format-patch -1 <commit_hash> and git format-patch main..feature (creates .patch files with mbox formatting)
Inspecting and Applying Patches: git apply --stat, git apply --check (dry run test), and git apply <patch_file>
Applying Patches with Full Commit Metadata: git am <patch_file> (recreates exact author, commit message, and timestamp)

modules.title: Debugging Regressions with Git Bisect & Binary Search
modules.summary: Master automated regression bug hunting with git bisect: binary search algorithm over commit histories in O(log N) steps, manual bisect workflow (start, good, bad, skip, reset), automated bisect testing with shell scripts (git bisect run), and combining bisect with git blame and pickaxe search.
topics: The Software Regression Nightmare: A feature that worked in v1.0.0 is broken in v2.0.0 across 800 historical commits
Why Linear Searching is Too Slow: O(N) manual checkout vs O(log2 N) Binary Search in Git
Mathematical Efficiency: Hunting through 1,024 commits takes only 10 test steps with git bisect!
Manual Git Bisect Workflow: 1) git bisect start, 2) git bisect bad (current broken commit), 3) git bisect good <known_working_commit>
Navigating Bisect Steps: Git automatically checks out the midpoint commit; testing and marking git bisect good or git bisect bad
Handling Untestable or Broken Commits: Skipping unbuildable commits using git bisect skip
Concluding the Bisect Session: Identifying the exact culprit commit (Author, Date, Commit Message, Diff) and resetting with git bisect reset
Automated Bisect with Test Scripts: Zero-manual-effort regression hunting using git bisect run <script.sh>
Writing Robust Bisect Test Scripts: Understanding exit codes (0 = Good, 1-127 = Bad, 125 = Skip / Cannot test)
Automating Node.js / Python / C Regression Tests with git bisect run npm test or pytest
Combining Bisect with Advanced Blame: Using git blame -C -C to track code copied from other files in the same commit

Diagnosing flaky tests or broken build configurations introduced by third-party dependency updates

Adding a Submodule: git submodule add <url> <path> and the .gitmodules configuration file
Cloning Repositories with Submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules vs running git submodule init && git submodule update
Submodule Pointer Mechanics: Understanding that the parent repo tracks only a specific commit SHA of the submodule, not a branch
Updating Submodules: Fetching upstream updates with git submodule update --remote and committing the new pointer in the parent repo

modules.title: Git Internals: Content-Addressable Storage & Object Database
modules.summary: Master the inner architecture of Git: Git is not a delta-based VCS, but a content-addressable key-value snapshot store. Explore the four core object types (blob, tree, commit, annotated tag), SHA-1/SHA-256 hash hashing mechanics, low-level plumbing commands (hash-object, cat-file, mktree, commit-tree), zlib compression, and manually building a commit from scratch.
topics: The Fundamental Insight: Git is a Content-Addressable Key-Value Snapshot Store with a VCS user interface!
Why Git Stores Snapshots, Not File Diffs: How Git reconstructs entire project states in O(1) time without replaying historical deltas
The 4 Core Git Object Types: 1) blob (raw file content), 2) tree (directories and file permissions), 3) commit (snapshot pointers and metadata), 4) tag (annotated references)
How Git Computes Object SHA-1 Hashes: The exact formula: SHA-1('type size\0content') and why identical file contents share the same blob SHA
Exploring .git/objects: The 2-character directory sharding structure and zlib compressed loose objects

Mastering Git Plumbing Commands: git hash-object -w (storing raw blobs), git cat-file -p (pretty printing objects), git cat-file -t (inspecting object types), and git cat-file -s (inspecting object sizes)
Deep Dive into Blob Objects: Storing pure content without file names, timestamps, or permissions
Deep Dive into Tree Objects: Mapping filenames, UNIX file modes (100644, 100755, 040000), and child blob/tree SHA hashes
Deep Dive into Commit Objects: Committer metadata, author metadata, timestamp, root tree SHA pointer, parent commit SHA pointer, and commit message
The Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG): Invariants, topological sorting, and mathematical properties of Git's history graph

topics: What are Git References (Refs)? Exploring .git/refs/heads/, .git/refs/remotes/, and .git/refs/tags/

Shrinking bloated repository clone sizes and repairing corrupted Git database objects

modules.title: Git Reflog, Dangling Commits & Complete Disaster Recovery
modules.summary: Master absolute disaster recovery in Git: The Reference Log (git reflog) safety net tracking every HEAD movement for 90 days, recovering from accidental git reset --hard, reviving deleted branches, restoring lost work after botched interactive rebases, undoing bad force pushes, and reviving orphaned commits with git fsck --lost-found.
topics: The Golden Maxim of Git: 'If you committed it at least once, it is almost impossible to lose in Git!'
What is the Reference Log (Reflog)? The local append-only flight recorder tracking every HEAD and branch pointer update
Where Reflogs Live: Inspecting .git/logs/HEAD and .git/logs/refs/heads/
Understanding Reflog Expiration Policies: Default 90 days for reachable refs, 30 days for unreachable refs (gc.reflogExpire)
Reflog Syntax and Navigation: HEAD@{0}, HEAD@{1}, branch@{yesterday}, HEAD@{2.hours.ago}, and git reflog show <branch>
Disaster Scenario 1: Accidental git reset --hard HEAD~5 -> Finding previous commit SHA in reflog and restoring with git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
Disaster Scenario 2: Accidental Branch Deletion (git branch -D feature) -> Finding the branch tip SHA in reflog and recreating with git switch -c feature HEAD@{N}
Disaster Scenario 3: Botched Interactive Rebase with Lost Commits -> Finding the pre-rebase commit SHA in reflog and resetting cleanly
Disaster Scenario 4: Undoing an Accidental Force Push (git push --force) -> Identifying pre-force-push commit on local or collaborator reflog and restoring with git push --force-with-lease
Disaster Scenario 5: Finding and Reviving Orphaned / Dangling Commits using git fsck --lost-found (reconstructing files from .git/lost-found/commit/)
Disaster Scenario 6: Corrupted .git Directory -> Rebuilding HEAD, index, and ref pointers manually from object database hashes
The Safe Alternative to Force Pushing: Always using git push --force-with-lease to prevent overwriting unseen remote commits
Classroom Emergency Drill: Sukanta Sir deliberately sabotaging students' repositories with hard resets, deleted branches, and rebase errors, challenging them to recover 100% of the code
Hands-on Terminal Lab: 8 simulated real-world disaster drills (hard reset, deleted branch, botched rebase, dropped stash, force push recovery) and restoring every single line of code
Self-Assessment Quiz & Short Questions for Module 005_003
learningOutcomes: Navigate and interpret git reflog entries across commits, resets, checkouts, and merges
Recover completely from accidental git reset --hard operations within seconds
Recreate deleted branches and recover lost stashes using reflog commit identifiers
Locate and reconstruct orphaned commits and blobs using git fsck --lost-found
miniProjects: Full-Spectrum Git Disaster Simulation & Automated Recovery Toolkit

assessment.type: Quiz + Live Disaster Recovery Exam (Zero-Data-Loss Requirement)

useCases: Serving as the senior 'Git Emergency Doctor' on engineering teams during production crisis situations
Restoring accidentally deleted team branches and reversing catastrophic developer force-pushes
commonMistakes: Panicking after git reset --hard and re-cloning the repository or making random edits, making reflog tracing more cluttered
Using git push --force instead of git push --force-with-lease on shared branches
Assuming that deleting a branch permanently deletes its commits immediately (commits remain safely in the object database for at least 30 days)
references: Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 10: Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery
Oh Shit, Git!?! (ohshitgit.com)
Official Git Documentation: git-reflog(1)
teachingTips: Have every student run git reset --hard HEAD~3 on purpose in class, and then guide them to type git reflog and git reset --hard HEAD@{1} to experience the thrilling magic of instant recovery.
Explain that reflog is strictly local to each developer machine and never gets pushed to GitHub.

modules.title: GitHub Actions, Automation & CI/CD Pipelines
modules.summary: Master CI/CD automation directly from Git: GitHub Actions architecture (Workflows, Events, Jobs, Steps, Runners), YAML workflow syntax (.github/workflows/*.yml), event triggers (push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch), test matrix builds, caching dependencies, managing secrets/environments, and automated deployments.
topics: Introduction to CI/CD in Modern Software Engineering: Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, and Continuous Deployment
GitHub Actions Core Architecture: Workflows (.github/workflows/*.yml), Events, Jobs, Steps, Actions, and Runners (GitHub-hosted vs Self-hosted)
Workflow Trigger Events: on: [push, pull_request], filtering by branches (branches: [main, develop]), paths (paths-ignore: ['**.md']), and scheduled crons (schedule: - cron: '0 0 * * *')
Manual Triggers with workflow_dispatch: Parameterized manual workflow runs from the GitHub UI
Essential Marketplace Actions: actions/checkout@v4 (cloning repo in runner), actions/setup-node@v4, actions/setup-python@v5, actions/cache@v4
Building an Automated Testing & Linting Pipeline: Running linters, unit tests, and build validation on every Pull Request
Matrix Builds: Running tests across multiple operating systems (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest) and language versions simultaneously
Managing Sensitive Secrets and Environment Variables: Repository Secrets, Environment Secrets, and referencing with ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
Job Dependencies and Conditional Execution: jobs.<job_id>.needs and if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
Automated Deployments: Deploying web applications automatically to Vercel, Netlify, AWS S3, or GitHub Pages on main merge
Automated Release Notes & Semantic Version Tagging via GitHub Actions
Classroom Project: Sachin, Mahima, and Susmita building an end-to-end full-stack automated CI/CD pipeline with test gates, PR blocking, and automated deployment
Hands-on Terminal & Web Lab: Writing a multi-job GitHub Actions workflow, configuring matrix tests, managing secrets, and verifying pull request test status gates

Pro Git (2nd Edition) - Chapter 6: GitHub - Automation

topics: Structuring Git Governance for Scale: From 5-person startups to 1,000+ engineer enterprise organizations
Standardizing Branch Naming Taxonomies: feat/JIRA-123-user-auth, bug/JIRA-456-cart-calc, chore/deps-upgrade, hotfix/auth-leak
